passage: Rafiq had just sat down in the school library when a burst of giggles came from the table behind him. He stiffened. Was it his haircut? His torn bag strap? He kept his eyes on his book and did not turn. Ms. Vinita, the librarian, glanced up from the desk. The giggling girls were bent over a phone screen, one of them holding up a cartoon. Rafiq still could not tell. He picked up his book, moved one table nearer to the desk, and decided he would watch for whether it happened again this week.

qa.q: Where was Rafiq sitting when the giggles started?
qa.a: In the school library, at a table in front of the girls.

qa.q: What was Rafiq worried about when he heard the giggles?
qa.a: He feared they were laughing at his haircut or his torn bag strap, though he had no proof, and the girls turned out to be looking at a cartoon on a phone.

qa.q: What could Rafiq do if the laughter did seem aimed at him again and again?
qa.a: He could tell Ms. Vinita or another trusted adult what he keeps noticing, instead of only guessing alone.

qa.q: How might Ms. Vinita see the situation?
qa.a: She sees girls sharing a joke on a phone and a boy who looks tense, so she may want to check quietly that he is all right. 🙂

grounding: A pupil hears tittering behind him, assumes it may be about him, but the cause stays ambiguous and reporting repeated targeting is hinted.

passage: Gurpreet was walking to the water cooler with her friend when she heard snickering from the back bench. Her steps slowed. She told me later that she felt every eye on her plaits. I was sitting two rows ahead, and I saw Nirmala's shoulders shaking as she read something inside her desk lid, a joke book passed from another class. Gurpreet's ears went red anyway. She drank fast and hurried back. I don't know what she thought, but she didn't look at that bench for the rest of the day, and I wondered whether anyone should tell her about the joke book.

qa.q: What was Nirmala reading inside her desk lid?
qa.a: A joke book passed from another class.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet probably feeling when she heard the snickering, and what else could explain her reaction?
qa.a: She probably felt self-conscious, since her ears went red and she hurried back, though she may also just have been thirsty and in a rush.

qa.q: What small step could help Gurpreet after this?
qa.a: She could quietly ask Nirmala or a friend what was funny, before deciding the laughter was about her.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel if she learned Gurpreet thought the snickers were about her?
qa.a: She would probably be surprised and a bit sorry, because she was only enjoying a joke book.

grounding: A pupil hears snickering that could be gossip or an unrelated joke, and the observer shows it was unrelated while her reaction stays visible.

passage: At break in Osaka, Sami saw Kaito sitting alone on the bench by the bike shed with his sleeve pressed to his face. Sami's first thought was to laugh, because Kaito never cried. Instead he stopped a few steps away. He could not tell whether Kaito was hurt, sad, angry or even relieved after the maths test. “Are you okay?” he asked. Kaito shrugged and sniffed. Sami sat down on the far end of the bench and unwrapped his rice ball, saying nothing more. After a while, Kaito wiped his eyes and pushed the bench a little to make room.

qa.q: Where did Sami find Kaito?
qa.a: On the bench by the bike shed.

qa.q: Why did Sami not laugh or guess when he saw Kaito crying?
qa.a: He realised he could not tell if Kaito was hurt, sad, angry or relieved, so he thought asking and staying close would be safer than deciding for him.

qa.q: What did Sami's quiet company do for Kaito?
qa.a: It gave Kaito space without pressure, and later Kaito made room on the bench, which suggests he was starting to feel a little better.

qa.q: What might Kaito have wanted from a classmate who found him crying?
qa.a: He may have wanted someone who did not tease or make him explain right away, and Sami's silence gave him that. 🙂

grounding: A child reads a crying classmate, cannot know the cause, and chooses asking and quiet company over laughing or guessing.

passage: The bell rang for lunch and Yogesh noticed that Swati was still at her desk, wiping her face with her hands. Two boys near the door started to smirk. Yogesh frowned at them and walked over. Swati might have been sad about her lost pencil box, or angry about the group project, or maybe she was just tired. He did not know. He crouched beside her chair. “Are you okay? I can sit here if you want.” Swati nodded a little without looking up. Yogesh took out his own sandwich and waited with her until Ms. Ramanathan came in.

qa.q: Who came over to Swati's desk?
qa.a: Yogesh walked over and crouched beside her chair.

qa.q: What was Yogesh thinking about why Swati was crying?
qa.a: He thought it might be sadness over her pencil box, anger about a group project or simple tiredness, and he admitted to himself that he did not know.

qa.q: Why was Yogesh's approach better than the smirking at the door?
qa.a: He asked and offered to stay, which respects her feelings, while smirking would have added embarrassment to whatever already hurt.

qa.q: How might Swati feel about the two boys and about Yogesh?
qa.a: She might feel exposed by the boys and comforted by Yogesh, since her small nod shows she accepted his company.

grounding: A classmate cries, the cause is uncertain, and the peer asks and stays quietly rather than laughing or guessing.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 5. Anirban came back from the playground with red eyes after he lost the relay. I watched him blink hard, turn towards the wall and ask, in a tight voice, to go and fill his bottle. He was gone six minutes. When he returned he sat down and opened his book without looking at his friends. I did not comment in front of the class. At the end of the period I told him quietly that tears are normal after a hard game, and that he can come to the corner near my desk whenever he needs a minute. He nodded. Dolma, Class Teacher.

qa.q: How many minutes was Anirban gone?
qa.a: Six minutes.

qa.q: What was Anirban probably feeling when he turned towards the wall and asked to fill his bottle?
qa.a: He was probably fighting back tears and feared being embarrassed in front of his friends, though he may also have been physically tired from running.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped, and what else could Dolma add?
qa.a: Dolma spoke privately and offered the corner near the desk, and Dolma could also check in with him later in the week.

qa.q: How might Anirban's friends see his walk to the wall?
qa.a: They may think he simply went for water and not notice he was upset, which is what he hoped for.

grounding: A schoolchild blinks back tears and leaves to avoid crying in front of peers, and a trusted adult normalises tears and offers private space.

passage: Tuesday night. I nearly cried in maths today. Mr. Sharma read out the marks and mine was the lowest in the row, and my eyes went hot. I stared hard at the ceiling fan and then asked to go to the bathroom. I washed my face and counted to ten. Preeti saw me when I came back and asked if I was okay. I said yes very quickly. I don't want anyone to think I'm a baby. Amma says crying is nothing to be ashamed of, but at school it feels different. Maybe I will tell Mr. Sharma tomorrow that I got upset. Jagdish.

qa.q: Who read out the marks in maths?
qa.a: Mr. Sharma.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish stare at the ceiling fan and go to the bathroom?
qa.a: Jagdish was afraid of being seen as a baby by classmates, so tried to hide the tears and recover privately.

qa.q: What could Jagdish do tomorrow to feel better about it?
qa.a: Jagdish could tell Mr. Sharma about getting upset, so a trusted adult knows and can offer a quiet place next time.

qa.q: How might Preeti have seen Jagdish on the return from the bathroom?
qa.a: Preeti noticed something was wrong and asked kindly, but the quick yes may have left Preeti unsure whether to ask again.

grounding: A schoolchild hides tears by looking away and going to the bathroom because of fear of embarrassment.

passage: The rain hammered the tin roof of the school hall, so the inter-house match was squeezed inside and everyone was packed shoulder to shoulder. When Chinmay's team missed a goal, someone near Thomas started to boo, and a few others joined in. Thomas felt the sound pull at him. Then he saw Chinmay by the goal post, staring at the floor with his jaw tight. Thomas kept his mouth shut. When Chinmay's team scored later, Thomas cheered loudly and clapped the goalkeeper, who grinned. Nobody could hear each other, but Chinmay looked up and found him in the crowd.

qa.q: Why was the match played inside the school hall?
qa.a: Because rain was hammering the roof.

qa.q: What was Thomas thinking when the booing started around him?
qa.a: He felt tempted to join in, but seeing Chinmay stare at the floor with a tight jaw made him think about how the booing landed on his friend.

qa.q: What did Thomas do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: He stayed quiet during the booing and cheered for a good play later, which showed friendly support without piling onto someone who was already upset.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt about the booing, compared with the cheering?
qa.a: The booing probably felt like jeering and added to his disappointment, while the cheer showed him someone was on his side.

grounding: A pupil hears booing and cheering at a match, considers the target's feelings and chooses not to join the jeering.

passage: “Booo!” The whole row of Class 6 yelled when Ishita walked out to bowl at the colony cricket day, and Aditi yelled too, laughing. But Ishita only bowed dramatically, and her team roared. Then the next over, Ishita's ball went wide and the booing grew louder and sharper. Aditi stopped. “Wait, that sounded different,” she whispered to her friend. Ishita's grin had gone stiff and she kept smoothing the ball on her shirt. Aditi walked to the boundary rope and called, “Come on, Ishita, you've got this!” 👏 Ishita glanced over and gave a small wave.

qa.q: Who did Aditi call out to from the boundary rope?
qa.a: Ishita.

qa.q: What did Aditi notice that made her stop booing?
qa.a: She heard the second round of booing as sharper and saw that Ishita's grin had gone stiff, so she thought it might no longer feel like friendly teasing.

qa.q: What could Aditi's friend do after hearing her whisper?
qa.a: The friend could join Aditi in cheering and choose friendly noise, since the same booing can be play one minute and hurtful the next.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt about the booing in the first over and the second?
qa.a: In the first over she played along as friendly rivalry, but by the second her stiff grin and fussing with the ball suggest it felt like pressure. 😔

grounding: Booing can be friendly rivalry or unkind jeering, and a child considers the target's feelings before joining in.

passage: From our balcony I saw the Class 4 boys near the gate and heard Charu yelling at another boy, his face red and his fists at his sides. “Give it back! Give it back!” The other boy just held a small green eraser high. I could not tell whether Charu was furious or scared, or simply wanted someone to listen. He didn't hit anyone. After a bit he stopped, turned and walked quickly to the guard's booth, still breathing hard, and said something to the guard, who walked back with him. The eraser was handed over. Charu's voice was shaking. I'm Rekha, his neighbour.

qa.q: What did the other boy hold up?
qa.a: A small green eraser.

qa.q: What might Charu have been feeling while he shouted, according to Rekha?
qa.a: Rekha could not be sure if he was furious, scared or just wanting to be heard, since his voice was loud and shaking but he did not hit anyone.

qa.q: What did Charu do that was safer than shouting back or fighting?
qa.a: He stepped away and went to the guard for help, which got the eraser returned without a fight.

qa.q: How might the other boy have seen Charu's shouting?
qa.a: He may have been startled, since a raised voice can feel threatening even when the shouter is scared or wants to be heard.

grounding: A child recognises shouting as anger, fear or a wish to be heard and responds by stepping back and getting an adult.

passage:
Monday. Harsha's brother shouted at him in the corridor before the bell, so loudly that Gargi jumped. Harsha shouted back, and it got worse. Gargi watched from the stairs and did not know what to do.

Wednesday. Harsha shouted at Gargi about a lost notebook. She felt her heart thump, but she said, “I'll help look,” in a low voice and took a step back. Harsha stopped, panting. It turned out he had been afraid of Sir's anger.

Friday. Someone shouted a threat at Gargi's cousin near the bus. She did not shout back. She found Mrs. Gomes straight away and told her.

qa.q: On which day did Harsha shout at Gargi about a lost notebook?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Harsha probably feeling when he shouted about the notebook?
qa.a: He was afraid of Sir's anger, and the shouting covered that fear.

qa.q: What did Gargi learn to do across the three days?
qa.a: She stayed calm and stepped back when Harsha shouted, and when a real threat was shouted at her cousin she reported it to Mrs. Gomes at once.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt when Gargi answered softly instead of shouting?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved and a little ashamed, since he stopped and was panting. 😔

grounding: Shouting can signal anger, fear or a wish to be heard, calm and stepping back are safer, and threats are reported.

passage:
On Monday Rajni's mother came home and let out a long sigh as she dropped her bag. Jasleen, sitting at her homework, felt her stomach drop. Did I do something? She stopped writing.

On Tuesday it happened again, and this time Jasleen asked, “Amma, is everything fine?”

Her mother blinked. “Oh, beta, the bus was packed and my feet hurt. That sigh was just tiredness.” She smiled. On Thursday Rajni's mother sighed again, dropped into the sofa and laughed, “That was relief. The report is finished!” Jasleen giggled and put her pencil back on the page.

qa.q: On which day did Rajni's mother explain that her sigh was tiredness?
qa.a: On Tuesday.

qa.q: What did Jasleen think when she heard her mother's first sigh, and why?
qa.a: She worried she had done something wrong, because she read the sigh as annoyance directed at her.

qa.q: What worked better than guessing, and why?
qa.a: Asking whether everything was fine, since the sighs turned out to be tiredness and relief and not anger at her.

qa.q: How might Rajni's mother feel when she learns Jasleen worried about her sighs?
qa.a: She might feel surprised and want to be clearer, since she never meant the sighs to be about Jasleen.

grounding: A schoolchild reads an adult's sigh as annoyance, then learns by asking that it was tiredness and relief.

passage: Aparna, my granddaughter, you asked why I always ask people, “Everything fine?” when they sigh. Let me tell you. When I was eleven, our teacher, Mr. Iyer, sighed loudly every time I read aloud. I decided I was a terrible reader and stopped putting my hand up. For a whole term I sat quiet. Years later I met him, an old man, and told him. He looked amazed. “Rukmini, I had a bad back that year! I sighed whenever I stood up.” I laughed and cried together. So now I ask. A sigh can be tired, bored, cross or glad, and I don't want any child to blame herself.

qa.q: How old was Rukmini when Mr. Iyer sighed at Rukmini's reading?
qa.a: Rukmini was eleven.

qa.q: Why did young Rukmini stop putting her hand up in class?
qa.a: Young Rukmini took the sighs to mean being a terrible reader, so felt discouraged and hid.

qa.q: What could a child do when a grown-up's sigh worries them?
qa.a: A child could ask something like “Is everything fine?” and not assume being the cause.

qa.q: How might Mr. Iyer have felt when he found out what Rukmini believed?
qa.a: He was amazed and probably sorry, because his sighs came from a bad back and had nothing to do with Rukmini's reading.

grounding: An elder recounts how a child read a teacher's sigh as annoyance, though it was tiredness, showing the ambiguity and value of asking.

passage: Freya was new at the school in Manchester, and when she told Alejandro she was from Chile he made a quick tsk sound with his tongue, and turned back to his lunch. Freya's face fell. In her town a tut like that could mean “no, I don't agree.” She said nothing. Then Alejandro added, still tutting softly, “Poor you, that's a long flight!” Freya blinked. In his family a tongue click meant “oh dear, I feel for you.” “Oh,” she said slowly. “I thought you were annoyed.” “No!” He laughed. “Sorry, that's how my grandmother sounds.”

qa.q: Where was Freya from?
qa.a: She was from Chile.

qa.q: Why did Freya's face fall when Alejandro tutted?
qa.a: In her town a tut like that could mean disapproval, so she took it as annoyance at her.

qa.q: What helped Freya and Alejandro sort out the mix-up?
qa.a: Freya said what she had thought and Alejandro explained his meaning, so they did not stay stuck on wrong guesses.

qa.q: How might Alejandro have felt on hearing that Freya thought he was annoyed?
qa.a: He may have felt surprised and a little embarrassed, since he had meant sympathy. 😅

grounding: A tut or tongue-click can mean disapproval in one place and sympathy in another, so a listener should not jump to conclusions.

passage: During the Class 5 morning assembly at a school in Pune, Deepak leaned over and whispered a wrong answer to the quiz question. Mahima, standing behind, gave a quick “tsk” and rolled her eyes to the ceiling. Deepak flushed. “She's annoyed with me,” he thought, and stared at his shoes. After assembly Mahima came up. “Sorry, I was tutting at myself. I forgot the answer too, and I felt silly.” In her family a tsk was for her own mistakes. Deepak let out a breath. “I thought it was for me,” he said, and they walked to class together.

qa.q: Where did the quiz happen?
qa.a: At the Class 5 morning assembly at a school in Pune.

qa.q: What did Deepak think Mahima's tsk meant, and what was it actually?
qa.a: He thought she was annoyed with him, but she was tutting at herself for forgetting the answer and feeling silly.

qa.q: What could Deepak try next time he is unsure about a sound like that?
qa.a: He could ask, “Was that about me?” before staying upset, because the same tut can carry different meanings.

qa.q: How might Mahima have seen Deepak's flushed face?
qa.a: She may have noticed he was embarrassed and realised her tsk could be misread, so she explained it.

grounding: A tongue-click can be disapproval, self-annoyance or something else, and a child checks before concluding.

subtype: Hmm, uh and um as thinking sounds [Expressing]
passage: Last week our teacher asked me what a noun is, and I said, “Hmm… uh… a noun is… um…” Some kids giggled. My hands went cold. I thought they believed I didn't know. But I did know, I just needed a moment to pick the right words. Miss waited, and I said, “A noun is the name of a person, place or thing.” She smiled and nodded. Later I told Aparna I say hmm when my brain is looking through its drawers. She said hers does too. Now I don't mind so much when the sounds slip out. I'm Rukmini and I like thinking time.

qa.q: What did the teacher ask Rukmini?
qa.a: What a noun is.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini say hmm, uh and um before answering?
qa.a: Rukmini knew the answer but needed a moment to choose words, so the sounds showed a mind at work, not a lack of knowledge.

qa.q: What could a teacher do to help a child who uses these sounds?
qa.a: She could wait a few seconds, like Miss did, so the child can finish the thought.

qa.q: How might the giggling classmates have seen Rukmini's hmm and um?
qa.a: They may have taken the sounds as not knowing, which is one way to read them, though the correct answer shows otherwise.

grounding: A schoolchild uses hmm, uh and um while thinking, and a teacher who waits gets a good answer.

subtype: Hmm, uh and um as thinking sounds [Expressing]
passage: Observation note, Class 4. Sarika was asked to explain why ice melts. She said, “Uh... hmm... it's because... um,” and looked at the window. Two classmates put up their hands. Usually I would have called on one of them within a moment. This time I counted silently and kept my eyes friendly. After what felt like a long while, Sarika said, “Because it gets warm and the water inside can move.” It was a thoughtful answer. I asked her what she had been doing in her head. She said, “Looking for how to say it.” I plan to wait longer with all pupils. Ms. Lavanya.

qa.q: What was Sarika asked to explain?
qa.a: Why ice melts.

qa.q: What did Sarika's hmm and um sounds suggest about what she was doing?
qa.a: She was thinking and searching for words, and she told the teacher she was looking for how to say it.

qa.q: What did the teacher change that helped, and what might she try next?
qa.a: Lavanya waited quietly instead of switching to another pupil, and she plans to wait longer with all pupils.

qa.q: How might the two classmates with their hands up have felt while waiting?
qa.a: They may have felt impatient because they knew their answers, but a short wait taught them that a thoughtful answer can arrive slowly.

grounding: Fillers like hmm, uh and um show the mind at work, and a teacher who waits gets a better answer.

passage: I used to think saying “ugh” was rude, but this week I learned it can mean lots of things. On Monday, Mummy told me to clean my fish tank and I said, “Ugh!” because the water smelled like old socks. On Wednesday, Kishore and I were working on a puzzle about a broken toy car. I stared and stared, and then I shouted, “Aha! The wheel goes on the other side!” Miss Reena clapped. I noticed that ugh means I don't like this, and aha means something suddenly made sense. I like aha more. Ujjwal.

qa.q: What did the water in the fish tank smell like?
qa.a: Old socks.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when Ujjwal said ugh on Monday?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt disgust at the smell of the tank and probably mild annoyance at having to clean it.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do about a chore that makes Ujjwal say ugh?
qa.a: Ujjwal could do it in small steps and keep going until it is done, or ask Mummy for help.

qa.q: How might Kishore have felt when Ujjwal shouted aha?
qa.a: Kishore may have felt excited and relieved, because the puzzle finally made sense.

grounding: A schoolchild says ugh at a chore and smell and aha at a discovery, showing disgust or annoyance versus sudden understanding.

passage: Teacher's note. During the science period today Yusuf lifted the lid of the compost bucket and said, “Ugh!” loudly, wrinkling his nose. Several children laughed and copied him. Later, while we built a model of the water cycle, he stared at the cloud made of cotton wool, then sat up straight. “Aha! The rain comes back to the river!” His whole face changed. I said, “That is a real discovery, Yusuf,” and asked him to explain it to the group. He did, slowly, and pointed at each part. I want to notice these moments more. Ms. Reena.

qa.q: What did Yusuf say when he lifted the compost bucket lid?
qa.a: He said “Ugh!” loudly and wrinkled his nose.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling at his ugh, and what changed at his aha?
qa.a: At ugh he felt disgust at the smell, and at aha he felt the sudden click of understanding, which his whole face showed.

qa.q: How did the teacher use Yusuf's discovery well?
qa.a: She named it as a real discovery and asked him to explain it to the group, so his understanding grew.

qa.q: How might the other children have felt when Yusuf explained his aha?
qa.a: They may have felt curious or proud of him, since some had laughed earlier and now saw he understood something.

grounding: A child says ugh at something smelly and aha at a discovery, and a teacher celebrates the aha.

passage: Sunday diary. Today in the Arts Hall Mr. Farooq talked about volcanoes, and his voice never went up or down, like a fan. I nearly fell asleep. Salma whispered, “He doesn't care.” But then I saw that he had dark circles and kept drinking water. Maybe he was very tired. Salma herself talks in a flat way when she is shy, and she cares a lot about everything. Then I remembered my cousin, who speaks in that flat voice all the time, and he loves his class and explains stuff beautifully. So a flat voice doesn't mean someone doesn't care. Kiran.

qa.q: What was Mr. Farooq talking about?
qa.a: Volcanoes.

qa.q: What did Kiran think about Mr. Farooq's flat voice, and what did Kiran notice?
qa.a: Kiran first felt sleepy and bored, but then noticed Mr. Farooq's dark circles and thought he might be tired, so stopped assuming he did not care.

qa.q: What could Kiran do if Kiran wants to understand a friend with a flat voice?
qa.a: Kiran could ask about the topic or watch what the friend does, not judge by tone alone.

qa.q: How might Salma have seen Mr. Farooq's voice?
qa.a: Salma took it as not caring, though Kiran suggests that could be wrong.

grounding: A pupil hears a flat, monotone voice and learns it may show tiredness, shyness or a speaking style, not a lack of caring.

passage: In the village school under the neem tree, Hansa's new teacher spoke in an even, soft voice and never smiled much. At first the children were unsure. Arohi whispered to Hansa, “She sounds cross.” Hansa shook her head. “She gave me her own pencil yesterday.” Later the teacher walked past every child's slate and quietly praised each drawing. When Arohi got hers praised, she looked shocked, then pleased. “Her voice is just like that,” Hansa said. “Maybe her voice is calm, or maybe she's tired. She isn't cross.” Arohi nodded and took her slate back to her seat.

qa.q: Where was the school?
qa.a: In a village, under a neem tree.

qa.q: Why did Hansa think the teacher was not cross, despite her flat voice?
qa.a: Hansa remembered the teacher giving her a pencil and saw her praising every drawing, so she trusted the actions more than the tone.

qa.q: What could Arohi try next time a teacher's voice makes her nervous?
qa.a: She could look at what the teacher does, like sharing pencils and praising drawings, and ask a question if she is still unsure.

qa.q: How might the teacher feel if children read her voice as cross?
qa.a: She might feel misunderstood, since her even voice is just how she speaks and she cares about her pupils.

grounding: A flat, even voice from a teacher is not proof of not caring, and the children learn to read actions along with tone.
